The '''Hilbert–Huang transform''' ('''HHT''') is a way to decompose a [[Signal processing|signal]] into so-called intrinsic mode functions (IMF) along with a trend, and obtain [[instantaneous frequency]] data.  It is designed to work well for data that is [[Stationary process|nonstationary]] and [[nonlinear]].

The Hilbert–Huang transform (HHT), a [[NASA]] designated name,<ref>{{cite book |editor-first1=Norden E. |editor-first2=Nii O. |editor-last1=Huang |editor-last2=Attoh-Okine |title=The Hilbert-Huang Transform in Engineering |date=2005 |doi=10.1201/9781420027532 |page=1 |isbn=978-0-429-11431-1 }}</ref> was proposed by [[Norden E. Huang]]. It is the result of the empirical mode decomposition (EMD) and the [[Hilbert spectral analysis]] (HSA). The HHT uses the EMD method to decompose a [[Signal processing|signal]] into so-called '''intrinsic mode functions''' ('''IMF''') with a trend, and applies the HSA method to the IMFs to obtain [[instantaneous frequency]] data. Since the signal is decomposed in time domain and the length of the IMFs is the same as the original signal, HHT preserves the characteristics of the varying frequency. This is an important advantage of HHT since a real-world signal usually has multiple causes happening in different time intervals. The HHT provides a new method of analyzing [[Stationary process|nonstationary]] and [[nonlinear]] [[time series]] data.

== Definition ==

=== Empirical mode decomposition ===
The fundamental part of the HHT is the '''empirical mode decomposition''' ('''EMD''') method. Breaking down signals into various components, EMD can be compared with other analysis methods such as [[Fourier transform]] and [[Wavelet transform]]. Using the EMD method, any complicated data set can be decomposed into a finite and often small number of components. These components form a complete and nearly orthogonal basis for the original signal. In addition, they can be described as intrinsic mode functions (IMF).<ref>{{cite web|last1=Lambert|first1=Max|last2=Engroff|first2=Andrew|last3=Dyer|first3=Matt|last4=Byer|first4=Ben|title=Empirical Mode Decomposition|url=https://www.clear.rice.edu/elec301/Projects02/empiricalMode/}}</ref>

Because the first IMF usually carries the most oscillating (high-frequency) components, it can be rejected to remove high-frequency components (e.g., random noise).<ref name="abvscan">{{cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Yangkang |last2=Ma |first2=Jitao |title=Random noise attenuation by f-x empirical-mode decomposition predictive filtering |journal=Geophysics |date=May 2014 |volume=79 |issue=3 |pages=V81–V91 |doi=10.1190/GEO2013-0080.1 |bibcode=2014Geop...79...81C }}</ref><ref name="emdsum">{{cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Yangkang |last2=Zhou |first2=Chao |last3=Yuan |first3=Jiang |last4=Jin |first4=Zhaoyu |title=Applications of empirical mode decomposition in random noise attenuation of seismic data |journal=Journal of Seismic Exploration |date=November 2014 |volume=23 |issue=5 |pages=481–495 |url=https://www.geophysical-press.com/journal/JSE/articles/286 }}</ref> EMD based smoothing algorithms have been widely used in seismic data processing, where high-quality seismic records are highly demanded.<ref name="enhemd">{{cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Yangkang|last2=Zhang|first2=Guoyin|last3=Gan|first3=Shuwei|last4=Zhang|first4=Chenglin|title=Enhancing seismic reflections using empirical mode decomposition in the flattened domain|journal=Journal of Applied Geophysics|date=2015|volume=119|pages=99–105|doi=10.1016/j.jappgeo.2015.05.012|bibcode=2015JAG...119...99C}}</ref><ref name="dipemd">{{cite journal|last1=Chen|first1=Yangkang|title=Dip-separated structural filtering using seislet transform and adaptive empirical mode decomposition based dip filter|journal=Geophysical Journal International|date=2016|volume=206|issue=1|pages=457–469|doi=10.1093/gji/ggw165|bibcode=2016GeoJI.206..457C|doi-access=free}}</ref>

Without leaving the time domain, EMD is [[adaptive algorithm|adaptive]] and highly efficient.<ref name="Huang, N. E. 1998">{{cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Norden E. |last2=Shen |first2=Zheng |last3=Long |first3=Steven R. |last4=Wu |first4=Manli C. |last5=Shih |first5=Hsing H. |last6=Zheng |first6=Quanan |last7=Yen |first7=Nai-Chyuan |last8=Tung |first8=Chi Chao |last9=Liu |first9=Henry H. |title=The empirical mode decomposition and the Hilbert spectrum for nonlinear and non-stationary time series analysis |journal=Proceedings of the Royal Society of London. Series A: Mathematical, Physical and Engineering Sciences |date=8 March 1998 |volume=454 |issue=1971 |pages=903–995 |doi=10.1098/rspa.1998.0193 |bibcode=1998RSPSA.454..903H |url=https://hal.science/hal-04014501 }}</ref> Since the decomposition is based on the local characteristic time scale of the data, it can be applied to [[nonlinear]] and [[Stationary process|nonstationary]] processes.<ref name="Huang, N. E. 1998"/>

=== Intrinsic mode functions ===
An '''intrinsic mode function''' (IMF) is defined as a function that satisfies the following requirements:
# In the whole data set, the number of [[maxima and minima|extrema]] and the number of zero-crossings must either be equal or differ at most by one.
# At any point, the mean value of the envelope defined by the local [[maxima and minima|maxima]] and the envelope defined by the local [[maxima and minima|minima]] is zero.

It represents a generally simple [[Oscillation|oscillatory]] mode as a counterpart to the simple [[harmonic]] function. By definition, an IMF is any function with the same number of [[Maxima and minima|extrema]] and zero crossings, whose envelopes are symmetric with respect to zero.<ref name="Huang, N. E. 1998"/> This definition guarantees a well-behaved [[Hilbert transform]] of the IMF.

=== Hilbert spectral analysis ===
[[Hilbert spectral analysis]] (HSA) is a method for examining each IMF's [[Instantaneous phase|instantaneous frequency]] as functions of time. The final result is a frequency-time distribution of signal amplitude (or energy), designated as the [[Hilbert spectrum]], which permits the identification of localized features.

== Techniques ==
The Intrinsic Mode Function (IMF) amplitude and frequency can vary with time and it must satisfy the rule below:
# The number of extremes(local maximums & local minimums) and the number of zero-crossings must either equal or differ at most by one.
# At any point, the mean value of the envelope defined by the local maxima and the envelope defined by the local minima is near zero.

=== Empirical mode decomposition===
[[File:Emd_example_lowres.gif|thumb|right|Illustration of Empirical Mode Decomposition's sifting process.]]

The empirical mode decomposition (EMD) method is a necessary step to reduce any given data into a collection of intrinsic mode functions (IMF) to which the [[Hilbert spectrum|Hilbert spectral]] analysis can be applied.

IMF represents a [[Simple harmonic motion|simple oscillatory mode]] as a counterpart to the simple [[harmonic]] function, but it is much more general: instead of constant amplitude and frequency in a simple [[harmonic]] component, an IMF can have variable amplitude and frequency along the time axis.

The procedure of extracting an IMF is called sifting. The sifting process is as follows:

# Identify all the local [[maximum and minimum|extrema]] in the test data.
# Connect all the local [[maxima and minima|maxima]] by a [[Spline (mathematics)|cubic spline line]] as the upper envelope.
# Repeat the procedure for the local [[maxima and minima|minima]] to produce the lower envelope.

The upper and lower envelopes should cover all the data between them. Their [[mean]] is ''m''<sub>1</sub>. The difference between the data and ''m''<sub>1</sub> is the first component ''h''<sub>1</sub>:

:<math>X(t)-m_1 = h_1.\,</math>

Ideally, ''h''<sub>1</sub> should satisfy the definition of an IMF, since the construction of h<sub>1</sub> described above should have made it [[symmetry|symmetric]] and having all [[maxima and minima|maxima]] positive and all [[maxima and minima|minima]] negative. After the first round of sifting, a crest may become a local [[maxima and minima|maximum]]. New [[maxima and minima|extrema]] generated in this way actually reveal the proper modes lost in the initial examination. In the subsequent sifting process, h<sub>1</sub> can only be treated as a proto-IMF. In the next step, ''h''<sub>1</sub> is treated as data:

:<math>h_{1} - m_{11} = h_{11}.\,</math>

After repeated sifting up to ''k'' times, h<sub>1</sub> becomes an IMF, that is

:<math>h_{1(k-1)} - m_{1k} = h_{1k}.\,</math>

Then, ''h''<sub>1k</sub> is designated as the first IMF component of the data:

:<math>c_1 = h_{1k}.\,</math>

=== Stoppage criteria of the sifting process===
The stoppage criterion determines the number of sifting steps to produce an IMF. Following are the four existing stoppage criterion:

==== Standard deviation ====
This criterion is proposed by Huang et al. (1998). It is similar to the [[Cauchy convergence test]], and we define a sum of the difference, SD, as
:<math>SD_k=\sum_{t=0}^{T}\frac{|h_{k-1}(t)-h_k(t)|^2}{h_{k-1}^2 (t)}.\,</math>
:Then the sifting process stops when SD is smaller than a pre-given value.

==== S Number criterion ====
This criterion is based on the so-called S-number, which is defined as the number of consecutive siftings for which the number of zero-crossings and [[minima and maxima|extrema]] are equal or at most differing by one. Specifically, an S-number is pre-selected. The sifting process will stop only if, for S consecutive siftings, the numbers of zero-crossings and extrema stay the same, and are equal or at most differ by one.

==== Threshold method ====
Proposed by Rilling, [[Patrick Flandrin|Flandrin]] and Gonçalvés, threshold method set two threshold values to guaranteeing globally small fluctuations in the mean while taking in account locally large excursions.<ref>{{cite conference |last1=Rilling |first1=Gabriel |last2=Flandrin |first2=Patrick |last3=Gonçalves |first3=Paulo |title=On empirical mode decomposition and its algorithms |date=2003 |url=https://inria.hal.science/inria-00570628/ |conference=IEEE-EURASIP Workshop on Nonlinear Signal and Image Processing NSIP-03 }}</ref>

==== Energy difference tracking ====
Proposed by Cheng, Yu and Yang, energy different tracking method utilized the assumption that the original signal is a composition of orthogonal signals, and calculate the energy based on the assumption. If the result of EMD is not an orthogonal basis of the original signal, the amount of energy will be different from the original energy.<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Junsheng|first1=Cheng|last2=Dejie|first2=Yu|last3=Yu|first3=Yang|title=Research on the intrinsic mode function (IMF) criterion in EMD method|journal=Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing|date=2006|volume=20|issue=4|pages=817–824|doi=10.1016/j.ymssp.2005.09.011|bibcode=2006MSSP...20..817J}}</ref>

Once a stoppage criterion is selected, the first IMF, c<sub>1</sub>, can be obtained. Overall, c<sub>1</sub> should contain the finest scale or the shortest period component of the [[Signal (electronics)|signal]]. We can, then, separate  c<sub>1</sub> from the rest of the data by <math>X(t)-c_1=r_1.\,</math> Since the residue, r<sub>1</sub>, still contains longer period variations in the data, it is treated as the new data and subjected to the same sifting process as described above.

This procedure can be repeated for all the subsequent r<sub>j</sub>'s, and the result is 
:<math>r_{n-1}-c_n=r_n.\,</math>
The sifting process finally stops when the [[residue (complex analysis)|residue]], r<sub>n</sub>, becomes a [[monotonic function]] from which no more IMF can be extracted. From the above equations, we can induce that
:<math>X(t)=\sum_{j=1}^n c_j+r_n.\,</math>

Thus, a decomposition of the data into n-empirical modes is achieved. The components of the EMD are usually physically meaningful, for the characteristic scales are defined by the physical data. Flandrin et al. (2003) and Wu and Huang (2004) have shown that the EMD is equivalent to a dyadic [[filter bank]].<ref name="dipemd"/><ref>{{cite journal |last1=Flandrin |first1=P. |last2=Rilling |first2=G. |last3=Goncalves |first3=P. |title=Empirical Mode Decomposition as a Filter Bank |journal=IEEE Signal Processing Letters |date=February 2004 |volume=11 |issue=2 |pages=112–114 |doi=10.1109/LSP.2003.821662 |bibcode=2004ISPL...11..112F }}</ref>

=== Hilbert spectral analysis ===
Having obtained the intrinsic mode function components, the [[instantaneous phase|instantaneous frequency]] can be computed using the [[Hilbert transform]]. After performing the Hilbert transform on each IMF component, the original data can be expressed as the real part, Real, in the following form:
:<math>X(t)=\text{Real}{\sum_{j=1}^n a_j(t)e^{i\int\omega_j(t)dt}}.\,</math>

== Current applications ==
=== Two-Dimensional EMD ===
In the above examples, all signals are one-dimensional signals, and in the case of two-dimensional signals, the Hilbert-Huang Transform can be applied for image and video processing in the following ways:

# ''' Pseudo-Two-Dimensional EMD (Pseudo-two-dimensional Empirical Mode Decomposition)''': 
#:Directly splitting the two-dimensional signal into two sets of one-dimensional signals and applying the Hilbert-Huang Transform separately. After that, rearrange the two signals back into a two-dimensional signal. 
#:The result can produce excellent patterns, and display local rapid oscillations in long-wavelength waves. However, this method has many drawbacks. The most significant one is the discontinuities, occurring when the two sets of processed Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) are recombined into the original two-dimensional signal. The following methods can be used to address this issue.
# ''' Pseudo-Two-Dimensional EEMD (Pseudo-two-dimensional Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition)''': 
#:Compared to Pseudo-Two-Dimensional EMD, using EEMD instead of EMD can effectively improve the issue of discontinuity. However, this method has limitations and it's only effective when the time scale is very clear, such as in the case of temperature detection in the North Atlantic. It is not suitable for situations where the time scale of the signal is unclear.
# ''' Genuine Two-Dimensional EMD (Genuine two-dimensional Empirical Mode Decomposition)''': 
#:As Genuine Two-Dimensional EMD directly processes two-dimensional signals, it poses some definitional challenges. 
::*How to determine the maximum value—should the edges of the image be considered, or should another method be used to define the maximum value? 
::*How to choose the progressive manner after identifying the maximum value. While [[Bézier curve]]s may be effective in one-dimensional signals, they may not be directly applicable to two-dimensional signals. 
::Therefore, Nunes et al. used radial basis functions and the [[Riesz transform]] to handle Genuine Two-Dimensional EMD. The following is the form of the Riesz transform. For a complex function f on <math>R^d</math>.
{{NumBlk|::|<math>R_jf(x) = c_d\lim_{\epsilon\to 0}\int_{\mathbf{R}^d\backslash
B_\epsilon(x)}\frac{(t_j-x_j)f(t)}{|x-t|^{d+1}}\,dt</math>|{{EquationRef|1}}}}
::for ''j''&nbsp;=&nbsp;1,2,...,''d''.
::The constant <math>C_d</math> is a dimension-normalized constant.
::<math>c_d = \frac{1}{\pi\omega_{d-1}} = \frac{\Gamma[(d+1)/2]}{\pi^{(d+1)/2}}.</math>

::Linderhed used Genuine Two-Dimensional EMD for [[image compression]]. Compared to other compression methods, this approach provides a lower distortion rate. Song and Zhang [2001], Damerval et al. [2005], and Yuan et al. [2008] used [[Delaunay triangulation]] to find the upper and lower bounds of the image. Depending on the requirements for defining maxima and selecting different progressive methods, different effects can be obtained.

=== Other application ===

*'''Nonstationarity detectors/methods for "stationarizing" time series based on HHT/EMD''': The EMD method can be used to develop nonstationarity detectors and method for "stationarizing" signals that are well-suited for analyzing complex time series with intricate temporal behaviors. By decomposing a signal into IMFs and a residual trend, EMD isolates components based on local time scales, without assuming linearity or stationarity. Each IMF can then be tested individually using conventional stationarity tests, allowing the detection (and further removal) of nonstationary components that may be obscured in the original signal. Also, the "good" properties of the IMFs regarding their approximately orthogonality and zero-mean characteristics make them suitable for probing nonstationary behaviors by means of decomposition.<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Eriksen |first1=Thomas |last2=Rehman |first2=Naveed ur |date=31 January 2023 |title=Data-driven nonstationary signal decomposition approaches: a comparative analysis |journal=Scientific Reports |volume=13 |issue=1 |page=1798 |doi=10.1038/s41598-023-28390-w  |doi-access=free|pmid=36721010 |pmc=9889333 |bibcode=2023NatSR..13.1798E }}</ref> This approach is particularly valuable for identifying complicated forms of nonstationarity, such as chirps, frequency-modulated components, or slowly-varying drifts,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Baptista de Souza |first1=Douglas |last2=Chanussot |first2=Jocelyn |last3=Favre |first3=Anne-Catherine |last4=Borgnat |first4=Pierre |date=1 February 2018 |title=A nonparametric test for slowly-varying nonstationarities |url=https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/abs/pii/S0165168417303171 |journal=Signal Processing |volume=143 |pages=241–252 |doi=10.1016/j.sigpro.2017.08.026 |bibcode=2018SigPr.143..241B |url-access=subscription }}</ref><ref>{{Cite book |last1=de Souza |first1=Douglas Baptista |last2=Chanussot |first2=Jocelyn |last3=Favre |first3=Anne-Catherine |last4=Borgnat |first4=Pierre |title=2014 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP) |date=May 2014 |chapter=A new nonparametric method for testing stationarity based on trend analysis in the time marginal distribution |pages=320–324 |doi=10.1109/ICASSP.2014.6853610 |isbn=978-1-4799-2893-4 }}</ref> which are difficult to capture using standard global tests. EMD-based methods thus provide a flexible framework for detecting nonstationarity in challenging real-world applications, including physiological signals, environmental measurements,<ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Peicai |last2=Wang |first2=Geli |last3=Bian |first3=Jianchun |last4=Zhou |first4=Xiuji |date=1 July 2010 |title=The prediction of non-stationary climate series based on empirical mode decomposition |journal=Advances in Atmospheric Sciences |volume=27 |issue=4 |pages=845–854 |doi=10.1007/s00376-009-9128-x |bibcode=2010AdAtS..27..845Y }}</ref><ref>{{Cite journal |last1=Kbaier Ben Ismail |first1=Dhouha |last2=Lazure |first2=Pascal |last3=Puillat |first3=Ingrid |date=September 2015 |title=Advanced Spectral Analysis and Cross Correlation Based on the Empirical Mode Decomposition: Application to the Environmental Time Series |journal=IEEE Geoscience and Remote Sensing Letters |volume=12 |issue=9 |pages=1968–1972 |doi=10.1109/LGRS.2015.2441374 |bibcode=2015IGRSL..12.1968K }}</ref> and financial time series<ref>{{cite patent|country=US |number=7464006 |title=Analyzing nonstationary financial time series via hilbert-huang transform (HHT) |inventor=Huang, Norden E.|gdate=2008-12-09}}</ref> where nonstationary patterns often evolve in non-standard and localized ways.

Results show the proposed algorithm provides no spurious IMF for these functions and is not placed in an infinite loop. EMD types comparison on ECG([[Electrocardiography]]) signals reveal the improved EMD was an appropriate algorithm to be used for analyzing biological signals.<ref>{{Cite book |last1=Ahmadi |first1=H. |title=2019 5th Iranian Conference on Signal Processing and Intelligent Systems (ICSPIS) |last2=Ekhlasi |first2=A. |year=2019 |isbn=978-1-7281-5350-6 |pages=1–5 |chapter=Types of EMD Algorithms |doi=10.1109/ICSPIS48872.2019.9066155 |doi-access=free}}</ref>

== Limitations ==
Chen and Feng [2003] proposed a technique to improve the HHT procedure.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Chen |first1=Yangbo |last2=Feng |first2=Maria Q. |title=A technique to improve the empirical mode decomposition in the Hilbert-Huang transform |journal=Earthquake Engineering and Engineering Vibration |date=June 2003 |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=75–85 |doi=10.1007/BF02857540 |bibcode=2003EEEV....2...75C }}</ref> The authors noted that the EMD is limited in distinguishing different components in [[narrowband|narrow-band]] signals. The narrow band may contain either (a) components that have adjacent frequencies or (b) components that are not adjacent in frequency but for which one of the components has a much higher [[energy]] [[intensity (physics)|intensity]] than the other components. The improved technique is based on beating-phenomenon waves.

Datig and Schlurmann [2004]<ref>{{cite journal|last1=Dätig|first1=Marcus|last2=Schlurmann|first2=Torsten|title=Performance and limitations of the Hilbert–Huang transformation (HHT) with an application to irregular water waves|journal=Ocean Engineering|volume=31|issue=14–15|pages=1783–1834|doi=10.1016/j.oceaneng.2004.03.007|year=2004 |bibcode=2004OcEng..31.1783D }}</ref> conducted a comprehensive study on the performance and limitations of HHT with particular applications to [[wind wave|irregular water waves]]. The authors did extensive investigation into the [[spline interpolation]]. The authors discussed using additional points, both forward and backward, to determine better envelopes. They also performed a [[parametric model|parametric study]] on the proposed improvement and showed significant improvement in the overall EMD computations. The authors noted that HHT is capable of differentiating between time-variant components from any given data. Their study also showed that HHT was able to distinguish between riding and carrier waves.

Huang and Wu [2008]<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Huang |first1=Norden E. |last2=Wu |first2=Zhaohua |title=A review on Hilbert-Huang transform: Method and its applications to geophysical studies |journal=Reviews of Geophysics |date=June 2008 |volume=46 |issue=2 |article-number=2007RG000228 |doi=10.1029/2007RG000228 |bibcode=2008RvGeo..46.2006H |doi-access=free }}</ref> reviewed applications of the Hilbert–Huang transformation emphasizing that the HHT theoretical basis is purely empirical, and noting that "one of the main drawbacks of EMD is mode mixing".  They also outline outstanding open problems with HHT, which include: End effects of the EMD, Spline problems, Best IMF selection and uniqueness.  Although the ensemble EMD (EEMD) may help mitigate the latter.

=== End effect ===
End effect occurs at the beginning and end of the signal because there is no point before the first data point and after the last data point to be considered together. However, in most cases, these endpoints are not the extreme value of the signal. Therefore, when doing the EMD process of the HHT, the extreme envelope will diverge at the endpoints and cause significant errors.

This error distorts the IMF waveform at its endpoints. Furthermore, the error in the decomposition result accumulates through each repetition of the sifting process.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Yang |first1=Guang |last2=Sun |first2=Xiang-Bin |last3=Zhang |first3=Ming-Xi |last4=Li |first4=Xiao-Li |last5=Liu |first5=Xin-Rong |title=Study on Ways to Restrain End Effect of Hilbert-Huang Transform |journal=電腦學刊 |date=October 2014 |volume=25 |issue=3 |pages=22–31 |url=https://csroc.org.tw/journal/JOC25-3/JOC25-3-3.pdf }}</ref> When computing the instantaneous frequency and amplitude of IMFs, Fast Fourier Transform (FFT) result may cause Gibbs phenomenon and frequency leakage, leading to information loss.

Here are several methods are proposed to solve the end effect in HHT:

==== 1. Characteristic wave extending method ====
This method leverages the inherent variation trend of the signal to extend itself, resulting in extensions that closely resemble the characteristics of the original data.
* Waveform matching extension:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Li |first1=Peng |last2=Gao |first2=Jing |last3=Xu |first3=Duo |last4=Wang |first4=Chang |last5=Yang |first5=Xavier |title=Hilbert-Huang transform with adaptive waveform matching extension and its application in power quality disturbance detection for microgrid |journal=Journal of Modern Power Systems and Clean Energy |date=January 2016 |volume=4 |issue=1 |pages=19–27 |doi=10.1007/s40565-016-0188-5 |doi-access=free }}</ref> 
: This extension is based on the assumption that similar waveforms repeat themselves within the signal. Therefore, a triangular waveform best matching the signal's boundary is identified within the signal's waveform. Local values within the signal's boundary can then be predicted based on the corresponding local values of the triangular waveform.
* Mirror extending method:
: Many signals exhibit internal repetition patterns. Leveraging this characteristic, the mirror extension method appends mirrored copies of the original signal to its ends. This simple and efficient approach significantly improves the accuracy of Intrinsic Mode Functions (IMFs) for periodic signals. However, it is not suitable for non-periodic signals and can introduce side effects. Several alternative strategies have been proposed to address these limitations.<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wang |first1=Jian |last2=Liu |first2=Wenyuan |last3=Zhang |first3=Shuai |title=An approach to eliminating end effects of EMD through mirror extension coupled with support vector machine method |journal=Personal and Ubiquitous Computing |date=July 2019 |volume=23 |issue=3–4 |pages=443–452 |doi=10.1007/s00779-018-01198-6 }}</ref>

==== 2. Data extending method ====
design and compute some needed parameters from the original signal for building a particular mathematical model. After that, the model predicts the trend of the two endpoints. 
* Support vector regression machine (SVRM) prediction:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Cheng |first1=Junsheng |last2=Yu |first2=Dejie |last3=Yang |first3=Yu |title=Application of support vector regression machines to the processing of end effects of Hilbert–Huang transform |journal=Mechanical Systems and Signal Processing |date=April 2007 |volume=21 |issue=3 |pages=1197–1211 |doi=10.1016/j.ymssp.2005.09.005 |bibcode=2007MSSP...21.1197C }}</ref>
: This method utilizes machine learning techniques to tackle the end effect in HHT. Its advantages are adaptive, flexible, highly accurate, and effective for both periodic and non-periodic signals. Although computational complexity can be a concern, disregarding this factor reveals SVRM as a robust and effective solution for mitigating the end effect in HHT.
* Autoregressive (AR) model:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Costa |first1=Antonio H. |last2=Hengstler |first2=Stephan |title=Adaptive time–frequency analysis based on autoregressive modeling |journal=Signal Processing |date=April 2011 |volume=91 |issue=4 |pages=740–749 |doi=10.1016/j.sigpro.2010.07.020 |bibcode=2011SigPr..91..740C }}</ref>
: By formulating the input-output relationship as linear equations with time-varying coefficients, AR modeling enables statistical prediction of the missing values at the signal's endpoints. This method requires minimal computational resources and proves particularly effective for analyzing stationary signals. However, its accuracy diminishes for non-stationary signals, and the selection of an appropriate model order can significantly impact its effectiveness.
* Neural network prediction:
: Leveraging the power of neural network learning, these methods offer a versatile and robust approach to mitigating the end effect in HHT. Various network architectures, including RBF-NN<ref>{{cite book |last4=Song Pu |last3=Li Yao |last2=Hong Jiang |last1=Jinghui Ma |title=2010 3rd International Conference on Computer Science and Information Technology |chapter=Notice of Retraction: End effects processing of Hilbert-Huang transform based on genetic algorithm and RBF Neural Network |date=2010 |pages=312–316 |doi=10.1109/ICCSIT.2010.5564604 |isbn=978-1-4244-5537-9 }}</ref> and GRNN,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Lv |first1=Chenhuan |last2=Zhao |first2=Jun |last3=Wu |first3=Chao |last4=Guo |first4=Tiantai |last5=Chen |first5=Hongjiang |title=Optimization of the End Effect of Hilbert-Huang transform (HHT) |journal=Chinese Journal of Mechanical Engineering |date=May 2017 |volume=30 |issue=3 |pages=732–745 |doi=10.1007/s10033-017-0101-9 |bibcode=2017ChJME..30..732L }}</ref> have emerged, demonstrating their ability to capture complex relationships within the signal and learn from large datasets.

=== Mode mixing problem ===
Mode mixing problem happens during the EMD process. A straightforward implementation of the sifting procedure produces mode mixing due to IMF mode rectification. Specific signals may not be separated into the same IMFs every time. This problem makes it hard to implement feature extraction, model training, and pattern recognition since the feature is no longer fixed in one labeling index. Mode mixing problem can be avoided by including an intermittence test during the HHT process.<ref>Hilbert-Huang Transform and Its Applications</ref>

==== Masking Method ====

Source:<ref>{{cite book |last2=James f. Kaiser |last1=Ryan Deering |title=Proceedings. (ICASSP '05). IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech, and Signal Processing, 2005 |chapter=The Use of a Masking Signal to Improve Empirical Mode Decomposition |date=2005 |volume=4 |pages=485–488 |doi=10.1109/ICASSP.2005.1416051 |isbn=0-7803-8874-7 }}</ref>

The masking method improves EMD by allowing for the separation of similar frequency components through the following steps:
#  ''' Construction of masking signal''': 
#:  Construct masking signal <math>s(n)</math> from the frequency information of the original data, <math>x(n)</math>. This masking signal is designed to prevent lower-frequency components from IMFs obtained through EMD.
#  ''' Perform EMD with masking signal''': 
#:  EMD is again performed on the modified signal x+(n) = x(n) + s(n) to obtain the IMF z+(n), and similarly, on x-(n) = x(n) - s(n) to obtain the IMF z-(n). The IMF is then defined as z(n) = (z+(n) + z-(n))/2 .
#  ''' Separation of Components''': 
#:  By appropriately choosing the masking signal frequency, components with similar frequencies can be separated. The masking signal prevents mode mixing, allowing EMD to distinguish between closely spaced frequency components.
#  ''' Error Minimization''': 
#:  The choice of parameters for the masking signal, such as amplitude, will affect the performance of the algorithm.

The optimal choice of amplitude depends on the frequencies
Overall, the masking method enhances EMD by providing a means to prevent mode mixing, improving the accuracy and applicability of EMD in signal analysis

====Ensemble empirical mode decomposition (EEMD)====

Source:<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Wu |first1=Zhaohua |last2=Huang |first2=Norden E. |title=Ensemble Empirical Mode Decomposition: A Noise-Assisted Data Analysis Method |journal=Advances in Adaptive Data Analysis |date=January 2009 |volume=1 |issue=1 |pages=1–41 |doi=10.1142/s1793536909000047 }}</ref>

EEMD adds finite amplitude white noise to the original signal. After that, decompose the signal into IMFs using EMD. The processing steps of EEMD are developed as follows:

#  Add finite amplitude white noise to the original signal.
#  Decompose the noisy signal into IMFs using EMD.
#  Repeat steps 1 and 2 multiple times to create an ensemble of IMFs.
#  Calculate the mean of each IMF across the ensemble to obtain the final IMF components.

The effects of the decomposition using the EEMD are that the added white noise series cancel each other(or fill all the scale space uniformly). The noise also enables the EMD method to be a truly dyadic filter bank for any data, which means that a signal of a similar scale in a noisy data set could be contained in one IMF component, significantly reducing the chance of mode mixing. This approach preserves the physical uniqueness of decomposition and represents a major improvement over the EMD method.

== Selection of relevant Intrinsic Mode Functions ==

Selecting relevant IMFs in EMD is important because not all IMFs carry meaningful or useful information for a given task, as some IMFs may correspond to noise, mode mixing, or undesirable residual trends. Since EMD is data-driven and adaptive, it decomposes a signal into IMFs ranging from high to low frequency, but without inherent guarantees that each IMF represents a physically interpretable or significant component. Low-order IMFs often capture high-frequency noise, while high-order IMFs may reflect low-frequency trends or artifacts. Therefore, identifying which IMFs to retain is essential to avoid reintroducing noise or discarding informative signal components. Several methods exist to guide IMF selection, including energy-based thresholds (e.g., retaining IMFs or a given subset of IMFs contributing significantly to the signal's energy<ref>{{cite book |last1=de Souza |first1=Douglas Baptista |last2=Chanussot |first2=Jocelyn |last3=Favre |first3=Anne-Catherine |title=2014 IEEE International Conference on Acoustics, Speech and Signal Processing (ICASSP) |chapter=On selecting relevant intrinsic mode functions in empirical mode decomposition: An energy-based approach |date=May 2014 |pages=325–329 |doi=10.1109/ICASSP.2014.6853611 |isbn=978-1-4799-2893-4 }}</ref>), entropy-based measures (such as permutation entropy or sample entropy<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Koppolu |first1=Pratap Kumar |last2=Chemmangat |first2=Krishnan |title=Automatic selection of IMFs to denoise the sEMG signals using EMD |journal=Journal of Electromyography and Kinesiology |date=December 2023 |volume=73 |article-number=102834 |doi=10.1016/j.jelekin.2023.102834 |pmid=37922679 }}</ref>), correlation with the original signal,<ref>{{cite journal |last1=Ayenu-Prah |first1=Albert |last2=Attoh-Okine |first2=Nii |title=A Criterion for Selecting Relevant Intrinsic Mode Functions in Empirical Mode Decomposition |journal=Advances in Adaptive Data Analysis |date=January 2010 |volume=2 |issue=1 |pages=1–24 |doi=10.1142/S1793536910000367 }}</ref> mutual information,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Mehboob |first1=Zareen |last2=Yin |first2=Hujun |title=Intelligent Data Engineering and Automated Learning - IDEAL 2009 |chapter=Information Preserving Empirical Mode Decomposition for Filtering Field Potentials |series=Lecture Notes in Computer Science |date=2009 |volume=5788 |pages=226–233 |doi=10.1007/978-3-642-04394-9_28 |isbn=978-3-642-04393-2 }}</ref> or task-specific relevance using supervised learning (e.g., feature importance in classification tasks).
